terms.short: Compare growth with inflation, the company's past, its sector and last year's base
terms.definition: A growth figure means little on its own. Check it against: inflation, since growth below inflation means the business shrank in real terms; the company's own record over the last three to five years; its sector peers in the same quarter, since a whole sector often slows together; and the base, since growth after a very weak year looks high and growth after a very strong year looks low. Use year-on-year rather than quarter-on-quarter for most companies, because many businesses are seasonal.
terms.note: Then ask where the growth came from: more volume, higher prices, an acquisition, or currency. Profit growing much faster than revenue usually means margins widened, or a one-off item: check other income and exceptional items before trusting it.
examples: Revenue up 8% looks fine, but with 5% price hikes and 5% inflation, volumes barely grew.

terms.short: Compare margins within a sector and watch the trend
terms.definition: Margins differ hugely by sector, so compare a company only with its peers: software and branded consumer companies often earn high operating margins, while retailers, traders and commodity processors earn thin ones and make money on volume. Within a company, the trend matters more than the level: rising margins can mean pricing power or operating leverage; falling margins can mean higher input costs, price cuts to defend share, or rising wages.
terms.note: A margin jump in one quarter may come from cheaper raw materials that won't last, or from one-off items. Gross margin shows pricing and input costs; EBITDA margin adds staff and overheads; PAT margin adds interest, depreciation and tax.
examples: A 7% EBITDA margin is normal for a supermarket chain and weak for an IT services firm.

terms.term: how to tell if profits are real
terms.short: Check cash flow, other income and one-off items
terms.definition: Reported profit can be flattered by things that won't repeat. Check three things. First, operating cash flow: over several years it should be close to net profit; profit that never turns into cash is a warning sign, often from rising receivables or inventory. Second, other income, such as interest on cash or gains on investments, which is not the core business. Third, exceptional items: one-off gains or losses that companies show separately.
examples: Profit doubled, but most of it was a one-off gain on selling land, so the core business was flat.

terms.term: how to judge a P/E ratio
aliases: is the PE high or low
terms.short: Compare P/E with the stock's own history, its peers and its growth
terms.definition: A P/E is high or low only by comparison. Compare it with the stock's own average over five to ten years, with similar companies, and with the market (the Nifty 50's own P/E). A higher P/E is reasonable for faster, steadier growth: the PEG ratio divides P/E by the growth rate to adjust for this. Sectors differ a lot: branded consumer companies usually trade at far higher P/Es than metals, PSU banks or oil companies.
terms.note: Traps: cyclical companies such as metals look cheapest on P/E at the top of the cycle, when profits are at a peak, and most expensive at the bottom. A P/E based on one-off profits misleads. Loss-making companies have no meaningful P/E. For banks and other lenders, price-to-book is the usual measure.
examples: At 25 times earnings the stock is below its own 10-year average of 32, but above its two closest peers.

terms.term: how to judge ROE and ROCE
aliases: return on equity good or bad
terms.short: Compare with the cost of capital, peers and the company's history
terms.definition: Return on equity and return on capital employed show how much profit a company makes on the money in the business. A business creates value only if these stay above its cost of capital, the return investors could expect elsewhere for similar risk. Returns that stay high for many years usually point to a real competitive advantage. Compare within a sector: capital-heavy businesses such as utilities and steel earn lower returns than software or branded consumer goods.
terms.note: ROE can be pushed up by heavy borrowing, so check debt-to-equity alongside it; ROCE includes debt and is the fairer measure for companies that borrow. For banks, look at return on assets as well as ROE.
examples: An ROE of 25% with almost no debt is much stronger than 25% with debt three times equity.

terms.term: how to judge a company's debt
terms.short: Check debt against equity, cash flow and interest bills, by sector
terms.definition: Look at debt in three ways: debt-to-equity (how much is borrowed against shareholders' money), debt compared with yearly operating profit or cash flow (how many years it would take to repay), and interest coverage (how many times operating profit covers the interest bill). The norm depends on the business: utilities and infrastructure firms with steady, contracted cash flows can carry more debt than cyclical companies, while many IT and FMCG companies have almost none.
terms.note: Rising debt is fine if it funds projects that will earn more than the interest; it is a warning sign when it funds losses or dividends. Banks and NBFCs borrow as their business, so these ratios don't apply to them; look at capital adequacy and bad loans instead.
examples: Interest coverage fell from 6 times to 1.5 times, so a small drop in profit could make the interest hard to pay.

terms.term: how to judge a dividend yield
terms.short: Check whether the payout is covered by profits and cash
terms.definition: Compare the yield with what safer options pay, such as fixed deposits, and remember that dividends are taxed at your income-tax slab rate. Then check whether it can last: the payout ratio (dividends as a share of profit) should leave room for the business, and free cash flow should cover the dividend. A yield far above the company's usual level often means the price has fallen because investors expect profits, and the dividend, to drop.
examples: Paying out 110% of profit, the company is funding its dividend from savings or borrowing, which can't last.

terms.term: how to read a big price move
aliases: why did my stock go up
terms.short: Check the news, the market and the sector before the company
terms.definition: First check whether the whole market or the sector moved the same day: if so, the cause is probably broad, such as interest rates, foreign investor flows or global news, not the company. If the stock moved alone, look for results, a change in guidance, a rating change by a brokerage, a large block deal, a regulatory order or promoter news. Remember the maths of losses: a stock that falls 50% must rise 100% to get back to where it was.
examples: The stock fell 6% while the Nifty IT index fell 5%, so most of the drop was sector-wide.

terms.term: how to judge a fund's returns
terms.short: Compare with the benchmark and category over several years
terms.definition: Judge a fund against its benchmark index and other funds in the same category, over three, five and ten years, not against a friend's fund in another category or last year's top performer. A fund that lags its benchmark for several years running, after costs, is a concern; one bad year is not. Rolling returns show how consistent it has been. Equity funds should be judged on five years or more.
terms.note: Compare like with like: direct plan with direct plan, and the same type of fund. A small-cap fund beating a large-cap fund in a rally says nothing about either manager.
examples: The fund returned 14% a year over five years, but its benchmark returned 15%, so it lagged after costs.

terms.term: how to measure my portfolio's return
terms.short: Use XIRR when money went in at different times
terms.definition: Absolute return is simply the total gain as a percentage of what you put in, and ignores time. CAGR gives a yearly rate for a single investment held from one date to another. When money went in and out at different times, as with a SIP, XIRR is the right measure, because it accounts for how long each rupee was invested. Compare the result with an index fund invested on the same dates, and with inflation for the real return.
examples: The SIP shows a 40% absolute gain, but spread over five years of instalments its XIRR is about 14%.

terms.term: how to read a fund's risk numbers
aliases: standard deviation sharpe beta in a factsheet
terms.short: Standard deviation, beta and Sharpe ratio, compared within a category
terms.definition: Factsheets show risk figures, usually over three years. Standard deviation shows how much the fund's returns swing; beta shows how much it tends to move when the market moves (above 1 means more); the Sharpe ratio shows return earned per unit of risk taken, so higher is better. Compare them only with funds in the same category, and alongside the riskometer and what the fund actually holds.
examples: Both funds returned 15%, but one had a much lower standard deviation, so it gave the same return with a smoother ride.

terms.term: how to read changes in shareholding
terms.short: Watch promoter stake and pledges, and institutions' moves over several quarters
terms.definition: The quarterly shareholding pattern shows who owns the company. A falling promoter stake can be harmless (selling to meet rules on public shareholding, or funding other plans) or a warning sign, so look for the reason. A rising share of pledged promoter shares is a risk, because a price fall can force lenders to sell. Steady buying by mutual funds or foreign investors over several quarters shows growing institutional interest; one quarter's change means little.
examples: Promoters cut their stake from 75% to 70% through an offer for sale to meet the minimum public shareholding rule.
